description.chief_complaint_and_history_of_present_i: Complete and concise, enabling the reader to fully understand what is happening “now” and the role of the pharmacy team
description.additional_background_and_findings: Complete and concise, enabling the reader to fully understand the data supporting later assessments, recommendations, and monitoring
description.condition_assessment_goals: Assesses condition control, acuity, and staging (if relevant) with reasonable accuracy and most goals conceptually included, but numeric targets for goals and/or data supporting the assessment (risk scores, modifiable risk factors or habits, etc.) frequently missing
description.medication_therapy_problems: Although most MTPs are identified and explained, there is an overall lack of connection between the type(s) of MTP identified and the provided assessment and recommendations
description.recommendations: Recommendations are appropriate and are likely to resolve further MTPs/benefit the patient, but some recommendations may lack proper specificity
description.monitoring: Most monitoring parameters for efficacy and toxicity are provided with reasonable timing, but parameters may not always be specific (e.g., lists lab panel name instead of desired lab) and/or includes unnecessary/excessive monitoring
description.rationale_and_citation_selection: Rationale and citations are generally appropriate, but may be missing for a few recommendations and/or some rationale lacks clarity/specificity
description.compositional_standards: Follows assignment parameters, avoids “do not use” abbreviations, and consistently attempts AMA style for in-text citations and reference list

nodes.title: CC/HPI
nodes.text:
PC is a 65 yo African American male presenting for follow-up after ED visit for chest pain. He now reports
acute, worsening left big toe pain and swelling for two days. In the ED, cardiac studies (EKG, troponin)
were normal, and he was diagnosed with stable angina. Cardiology follow-up for exercise stress test and
left heart cath confirmed stable angina; diltiazem and sublingual nitroglycerin were initiated. Chest pain
(8/10) is continued, predictable with exertion (≥ 2 flights of stairs), and resolves with 10-15 minutes of rest
or nitroglycerin. He seeks improved tolerance to climb stairs further and faster.

nodes.title: Additional Background & Findings
nodes.text:
Several months ago, PC presented with chest pain that resolved with rest, diagnosed with angina and
given SL NTG. Initial cardiology visit on 10/11/24 diagnosed him with stable ischemic heart disease and
initiated diltiazem XR daily and ezetimibe daily. Relevant PMH includes CCD, HTN, stage 3B CKD (SCr
1.6-1.7), and HLD. Past surgical history includes appendectomy (age 27) and inguinal hernia (age 41).
Socially, PC is married, drinks wine with dinner once a week, and has occasional beer with friends on
weekends. He is a current smoker of 1 pack of cigarettes/day, and reports that he started sometime
during his teens. PC recently retired from being a plumber and has Cigna Plus 5-Tier insurance. His
family history includes his mother with dementia, HTN, TIA (age 54) - alive at age 96, and father with MI
(age 52) and prostate cancer (died age 75). PC reports an allergy to atorvastatin (ADR of muscle pain).
He is up to date on pneumococcal, zoster, influenza, and COVID vaccines.
Diagnostics: (09/20/2024) ECHO: LVEF 68%, ECG: NSR, no ST changes (10/02/2024) Exercise Stress
Test - pt stressed by continuous graded treadmill testing for nine minutes, HR increased from 94 to 178
BPM, which is 100% of maximum predicted HR, BP increased from 128/78 to 152/90 SBP/DBP, revealed
regular sinus rhythm, symptoms of chest pain occurs with exercise but is reversible with rest. Positive for
ischemic. (10/04/2024) Left Heart Catheterization - left anterior descending: prox LAD and mid LAD lesion
is 75% stenosed, left circumflex, prox Cx lesion is 40% stenosed, right coronary artery: vessel is clear.
Interpretation: coronary artery disease present in LAD and LCx, drug eluting stent (DES) not placed
Current medications include aspirin 81 mg PO daily, diltiazem 120 mg XR PO daily, ezetimibe 10 mg PO
daily, metformin 500 mg PO BID, rosuvastatin 40 mg daily, SL NTF 0.4 mg PRN and triamterene-HCTZ
75/50 mg PO daily.
PE: Vital signs (02/18): BP 141/92 mmHg (147/86 on 10/11/24, 142/88 on 09/20/2024), HR 72 bpm, RR
12 bpm, Temp 98.6°F, Ht 70 in, Wt 103 kg, BMI 32.3.
Cardiovascular: RRR, normal S1 and S2, no murmur, no JVD, musculoskeletal: normal strength in lower
extremities, genitalia/rectum: DRE - smooth prostate, no nodules.
Labs: SCr 1.7mg/dL, GFR 52.9 mL/min, CrCl 52mL/min, Glucose 87 mg/dL (decreased from 109 on
09/19), Potassium 4.6 mg/dL (increased from 3.6 on 9/19/24), Chloride 100 mg/dL, Sodium 142 mg/dL,
Calcium 9.1 mg/dL, HDL 36 mg/dL, LDL 82 mg/dL (decreased from 98 on 10/11 and 185 on 07/16), TG
124 mg/dL, Total Cholesterol 126 mg/dL, HbA1C 7.6%, Uric acid level 9.1 mg/dL. Negative troponin and
BNP 65 pg/mL on 09/19. CBC with differential (09/19) showed WBC 7,000 cells/mL, Hemoglobin 14 g/dL,
Hematocrit 43%, and Platelet Count of 238,000.

nodes.title: Assessment & Goals
nodes.text:
PC continues to experience predictable chest pain when needing to climb more
than two flights of stairs, placing him at the Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) Class II grading.
Stable angina symptoms are controlled retroactively, but PC is requesting proactive symptom control.
LDL, BP, and A1C are above Goals, possibly contributing to angina symptoms and placing PC at risk for
ASCVD events. Short-term Goals include reducing the number of angina episodes, alleviating symptoms
of angina (i.e. chest pain), lowering BP (< 130/80 mmHg) and LDL (< 70 mg/dL), and educating the
patient on the benefits of smoking cessation and implementing the DASH diet. Long-term Goals include
improving patient QoL, preventing MI, reducing hospitalizations, mortality, and morbidity as well as
maintaining LDL, BP, and A1C Goals.

nodes.title: Medication Therapy Problems
nodes.text:
* Indication - Needs additional drug therapy - Preventative therapy (SL NTG)
* Safety - Adverse drug reaction - Drug unsafe for patient (diltiazem)
* Indication - Needs additional drug therapy - Synergistic therapy (rosuvastatin)
* Indication - Needs additional drug therapy - Synergistic therapy (metformin)
* Indication - Need additional drug therapy - Synergistic Therapy (carvedilol)

nodes.title: Recommendations
nodes.text:
* START carvedilol IR 12.5 mg PO BID; Increase dose as tolerated by doubling the current dose
until optimal clinical response or heart rate <55 bpm; Max dose of 50 mg BID
* STOP diltiazem 120 mg XR PO daily. START amlodipine 5 mg PO daily. Assess response and
tolerance to amlodipine in 2-4 weeks. Titrate up to a max dose of 10 mg PO daily as needed.
* START evolucomab 140mg SubQ every 2 weeks. Titrate every 2 weeks as tolerated to Goals LDL
(maximum dose of 420 mg every 2 weeks).
* CONTINUE metformin 500 mg PO BID. START empagliflozin 10 mg PO once daily. Titrate to 25
mg in 4-6 weeks as tolerated to reach A1C Goals of <7%.
* CONTINUE aspirin 81 mg PO once daily.
* RECOMMEND lifestyle modifications including DASH diet, light exercise, and smoking cessation.

nodes.title: Monitoring
nodes.text:
Follow-up in 2 weeks when PC receives second dose of evolocumab. Assess medication efficacy and
toxicity; frequency and severity of angina. Monitor for achieving Goals BP <130/80, maintenance of fasting
blood glucose between 80 and 130 mg/dL, BP for hypotension, HR, BMP (SCr, glucose, K, BUN), weight
gain, diarrhea every 2 weeks. Monitor for injection site reaction (i.e., erythema, pruritus, pain at injection
site), and for hypersensitivity reaction (i.e., swelling of tongue and/or throat, hives, difficulty breathing)
after first injection of alirocumab and first dose of empagliflozin. Monitor for Goals A1c <7% in 3 months,
and Goals LDL <70 mg/dL in 4 weeks. Counsel PC to monitor for urinary tract and fungal infection (i.e.,
itching around genitalia, burning while urinating), symptoms of SSTI (i.e., redness, inflammation, hot to
touch, purulence if skin has been broken), and symptoms of ketoacidosis (i.e., N/V, abdominal pain,
malaise, shortness of breath. Monitor blood volume (i.e., hematocrit) in 2 weeks. Counsel pt to monitor for
symptoms of GI bleeding (i.e., melena, hematemesis) or bleeding events (e.g., nosebleed that will not
stop). Counsel PC and wife on DASH diet, incorporating light exercise of walking or dancing 10-20
minutes 5 times per week as tolerated, and smoking cessation using NRT as needed. Educate and
advise pt to continue Monitoring blood pressure twice a day and blood glucose daily; keeping a journal.

nodes.title: Rationale
nodes.text:
PC does not have any indication for oral anticoagulant therapy, and thus should continue taking low-dose
81 mg aspirin daily to reduce the risk of atherosclerotic events.1,2 PC continues to experience symptoms
related to CCD, including angina, while taking diltiazem, a calcium channel blocker, so a beta blocker,
carvedilol, should be initiated for further symptom management.1,3 Carvedilol will help to further lower BP
towards Goals of 130/80 mmHg as well as its ability to reduce the risk of CV events.4 In addition, carvedilol
is recommended due to its concomitant vasodilatory effect and less adverse metabolic effects, and it is
associated with improved insulin sensitivity and less progression to microalbuminuria (can worsen
glycemic control and increase insulin resistance) compared to metoprolol.4,5 Amlodipine, a dihydropyridine
calcium channel blocker, is recommended over the current non-DHP CCB of diltiazem because of the
patient’s uncontrolled HTN with CCD, due to the risk of heart block and bradycardia in combo non-DHP
CCB and BB therapy.4
PC is already taking the maximum tolerated dose of rosuvastatin as well as ezetimibe; thus, a PCSK9
monoclonal antibody is an appropriate add-on to reduce cardiovascular risk and achieve LDL Goals.6,7,8
Alternative agents, such as bempedoic acid or inclisiran, should be considered for patients who remain
above their target LDL levels despite treatment with a maximally tolerated statin, ezetimibe, and a PCSK9
monoclonal antibody, per guideline recommendations.7 Lifestyle modifications that support a healthy
weight, including adherence to a heart-healthy diet (DASH diet) and regular physical activity, can improve
obesity-related cardiovascular comorbidities, and should be encouraged for all patients with
cardiovascular disease.2 Smoking cessation has been shown to reduce mortality and myocardial
infarction risk in this patient population.9 Tobacco smoke exposure is a major contributor to CVD and
cardiovascular events in individuals with CVD.2,10 Patients should be counseled on the importance of
smoking cessation, and behavioral and/or pharmacologic interventions should be considered as needed
to support cessation efforts.

nodes.title: Assessment & Goals
nodes.text:
PC has new acute pain and swelling in left big toe which began suddenly two days ago and is worsening,
as well as a high uric acid level (9.1 mg/dL), suggesting acute, uncontrolled gout flare. Potential
contributing factors include use of loop and thiazide diuretics for treatment of HTN, as well as poor renal
function, CKD, obesity, and lifestyle. PC requires immediate treatment for gout flare. Short-term Goals
include resolving the acute gout flare and returning PC to baseline QoL. Long-term Goals include
preventing recurrence of gout flares, maintaining uric acid levels under 6 mg/dL, preventing complications
associated with chronic deposition of uric acid crystals, and reducing the risk of urolithiasis and worsening
of kidney function.

nodes.title: Medication Therapy Problems
nodes.text:
* Indication - Needs additional drug therapy - Untreated condition (gout flare)
* Indication - Needs additional drug therapy - Preventative therapy (allopurinol)
* Safety - Adverse medication event - Undesirable effect (triamterene-HCTZ)

nodes.title: Recommendations
nodes.text:
* STOP triamterene-HCTZ 75/50mg PO QD. START losartan 50mg QD. Titrate losartan as
tolerated every 2 weeks to Goals BP <130/80 or maximum dose 100mg PO QD.
* START colchicine 1.2 mg initially, followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later for acute gout flare.
* Following treatment of acute gout flare, START colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily for 3 months as
anti-inflammatory gout prophylaxis during initiation of pharmacologic urate lowering therapy.
* RECOMMEND PGx testing for HLA-B *5801 allele before beginning urate lowering therapy. If
allele is not present, START allopurinol 50 mg daily. Titrate up in 100 mg increments every 4
weeks to max of 800 mg as needed to achieve serum urate concentration <6 mg/dL.
* RECOMMEND lifestyle modifications including DASH Diet, weight loss, reduction in alcohol
consumption, and reduction in smoking.
. If a co-morbid condition impacts your recommendation, please include that in
the Rationale.
The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) guidelines recommend NSAIDs, corticosteroids, or
colchicine as first-line monotherapy options in the management of acute gout flares.11 For PC, NSAIDs
are not preferred due to impaired renal function, as they may exacerbate kidney injury.12,13 Corticosteroids
were not chosen due to the patient’s T2DM, given the potential for hyperglycemia with steroid use.12,13
Colchicine was selected as the preferred treatment due to its more favorable safety profile, but a dose
adjustment was required due to the concomitant use of diltiazem, a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor, which
can increase colchicine plasma concentrations and the risk of toxicity.11 Colchicine is recommended as
prophylactic therapy during the initiation of allopurinol for the first 3 to 6 months to reduce the risk of gout
flares and improve adherence to urate-lowering therapy (ULT), per ACR guidelines.11,13
Given the association between diuretics and increased serum uric acid levels, losartan was
recommended as an alternative antihypertensive agent to triamterene-HCTZ.14 Losartan possesses
uricosuric properties that promote significant uric acid excretion while effectively managing blood
pressure.14 As an angiotensin II receptor blocker, losartan provides renoprotective effects that benefit
patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), and its ability to lower serum uric acid levels has been linked
to long-term renal risk reduction.15 Due to the patient’s first gout flare occurring in the setting of CKD stage
3b and a serum uric acid level greater than 9 mg/dL, initiation of ULT is recommended.11 Allopurinol is the
preferred first-line ULT, with a starting dose of 50 mg daily given the patient’s CrCl of less than 60
mL/min.11 However, due to the patient’s African American descent, HLA-B *5801 testing is recommended
before initiation to assess the risk of severe cutaneous adverse reactions; if the test is positive, an
alternative ULT would be considered.16 Lifestyle modifications, including reducing alcohol consumption,
smoking cessation, and weight management, along with adhering to the DASH diet, can help decrease
the frequency of gout flares and mitigate potential complications associated with the disease.17,18,19

nodes.title: Monitoring
nodes.text:
should include assessing the resolution of pain and Monitoring complete blood
count (CBC). For toxicity, gastrointestinal adverse effects such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea should
be observed, along with the rare but serious risks of myelosuppression and reversible neuromyopathy,
which may be exacerbated by the patient’s statin therapy and impaired kidney function. Renal function
should be closely monitored with regular basic metabolic panel (BMP) assessments, including SCr and K,
as well as BP Monitoring for hypotension. SCr should be evaluated every two weeks, with immediate
discontinuation of therapy if SCr increases by more than 30% within one week. Patients should also be
counseled on recognizing symptoms of angioedema, such as difficulty breathing, tongue swelling, or
throat swelling, and should be advised to discontinue losartan immediately and seek medical attention if
these occur. Additionally, lifestyle modifications should be emphasized to help reduce the risk of gout
flares, including adherence to the DASH diet, weight loss, limiting alcohol consumption, and smoking
cessation. Patients should be provided with strategies and resources to support these behavioral
changes.

nodes.text: START colchicine 1.2 mg initially, followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later for acute gout flare.

nodes.title: Recommendations
nodes.text: Following treatment of acute gout flare, START colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily for 3 months as anti-inflammatory gout prophylaxis during initiation of pharmacologic urate lowering therapy.

nodes.title: Recommendations
nodes.text: RECOMMEND PGx testing for HLA-B *5801 allele before beginning urate lowering therapy. If allele is not present, START allopurinol 50 mg daily. Titrate up in 100 mg increments every 4 weeks to max of 800 mg as needed to achieve serum urate concentration <6 mg/dL.

nodes.title: Recommendations
nodes.text: RECOMMEND lifestyle modifications including DASH Diet, weight loss, reduction in alcohol consumption, and reduction in smoking. . If a co-morbid condition impacts your recommendation, please include that in the Rationale. The American College of Rheumatology (ACR) guidelines recommend NSAIDs, corticosteroids, or colchicine as first-line monotherapy options in the management of acute gout flares.11 For PC, NSAIDs are not preferred due to impaired renal function, as they may exacerbate kidney injury.12,13 Corticosteroids were not chosen due to the patient’s T2DM, given the potential for hyperglycemia with steroid use.12,13 Colchicine was selected as the preferred treatment due to its more favorable safety profile, but a dose adjustment was required due to the concomitant use of diltiazem, a moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor, which can increase colchicine plasma concentrations and the risk of toxicity.11 Colchicine is recommended as prophylactic therapy during the initiation of allopurinol for the first 3 to 6 months to reduce the risk of gout flares and improve adherence to urate-lowering therapy (ULT), per ACR guidelines.11,13 Given the association between diuretics and increased serum uric acid levels, losartan was recommended as an alternative antihypertensive agent to triamterene-HCTZ.14 Losartan possesses uricosuric properties that promote significant uric acid excretion while effectively managing blood pressure.14 As an angiotensin II receptor blocker, losartan provides renoprotective effects that benefit patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), and its ability to lower serum uric acid levels has been linked to long-term renal risk reduction.15 Due to the patient’s first gout flare occurring in the setting of CKD stage 3b and a serum uric acid level greater than 9 mg/dL, initiation of ULT is recommended.11 Allopurinol is the preferred first-line ULT, with a starting dose of 50 mg daily given the patient’s CrCl of less than 60 mL/min.11 However, due to the patient’s African American descent, HLA-B *5801 testing is recommended before initiation to assess the risk of severe cutaneous adverse reactions

nodes.title: Recommendations
nodes.text: if the test is positive, an alternative ULT would be considered.16 Lifestyle modifications, including reducing alcohol consumption, smoking cessation, and weight management, along with adhering to the DASH diet, can help decrease the frequency of gout flares and mitigate potential complications associated with the disease.17,18,19

nodes.title: Monitoring
nodes.text: should include assessing the resolution of pain and Monitoring complete blood count (CBC).

nodes.title: Monitoring
nodes.text: For toxicity, gastrointestinal adverse effects such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea should be observed, along with the rare but serious risks of myelosuppression and reversible neuromyopathy, which may be exacerbated by the patient’s statin therapy and impaired kidney function.

nodes.title: Monitoring
nodes.text: Renal function should be closely monitored with regular basic metabolic panel (BMP) assessments, including SCr and K, as well as BP Monitoring for hypotension.

nodes.title: Monitoring
nodes.text: SCr should be evaluated every two weeks, with immediate discontinuation of therapy if SCr increases by more than 30% within one week.

nodes.title: Monitoring
nodes.text: Patients should also be counseled on recognizing symptoms of angioedema, such as difficulty breathing, tongue swelling, or throat swelling, and should be advised to discontinue losartan immediately and seek medical attention if these occur.

nodes.title: Monitoring
nodes.text: Additionally, lifestyle modifications should be emphasized to help reduce the risk of gout flares, including adherence to the DASH diet, weight loss, limiting alcohol consumption, and smoking cessation.

nodes.title: Monitoring
nodes.text: Patients should be provided with strategies and resources to support these behavioral changes.
